title: Let the children come (Mark 10:1–16)
hookLine: the disciples shoo the children, and he is indignant

cards: An important visitor comes to town, and a security detail keeps the crowd back. Somewhere at the edge, kids are trying to get through.
Jesus has crossed into Judea, on the far side of the Jordan, heading south toward Jerusalem. Crowds again. Teachers come with a hard question about marriage.
In the middle of all this serious business, parents bring their children for him to touch. The disciples scold them. He's busy.
Not now. And Mark tells us Jesus was indignant.

teach.b: First, the question before it. Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife. Jesus goes back past the Law to the beginning, to Genesis: God made them male and female, and the two become one flesh.
What God has joined, no one should separate. Catholics hear in these verses the root of the Church's teaching that a sacramental marriage is for life.
Other Christians read the passage in other ways, and it can be a tender subject in families. Mark gives it a few lines and moves on. Second, the scolding.
The disciples rebuke the people bringing children. Maybe they're protecting him. Maybe kids just weren't important enough.
Either way, they've already forgotten yesterday. Third, his anger. Mark's word is strong: much displeased, indignant.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer is old English for allow.
Then he goes further: whoever doesn't receive the kingdom of God like a little child won't enter it. Not earned, like a grown-up. Handed over, like a child being given it.
"And embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them."
The Catechism quotes these words when it speaks of children and the sacraments.

teach.h: OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.
teach.b: The Church baptizes infants, who can't earn anything, and simply receive.

how: The Catholic Church baptizes infants, and in some parishes children too young for Communion come forward for a blessing; Mark 10:13–16 is among the passages that may be read at infant baptisms.

o: embarrassed in front of a big crowd
tired and wanting to be left alone
angry at something wrong or unfair

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus says the kingdom must be received like a little child
whoever doesn't receive it as a little child won't enter it.
suffer the little children means let them suffer
suffer is old English for allow: let them come.
Jesus tells the children to wait until he's finished teaching
he embraces them, lays his hands on them and blesses them.

games.q: you're a disciple. Jesus is in the middle of serious teaching, and parents keep pushing their kids forward. what do you do?
o: tell the parents to take the children away.
line the children up to meet him.
games.why: the disciples scold the parents, and Jesus is indignant: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not."

practice: Open your hands, palms up, on your lap: a child doesn't earn a hug or a meal, they just receive.

Think of something good you've been handed lately and never quite received, a compliment you brushed off, help you felt you had to pay back, love you didn't think you'd earned, and let it land with a thank you, out loud or inside.
If you pray, you can receive it as a gift from God.

wordCard.voice: Indignant. What Jesus felt, strongly, when his disciples tried to send the children away: anger at a wrong, right before he blessed them. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he was indignant, much displeased: anger at a wrong.

carryVoice: Your line: of such is the kingdom. Nobody earns a blessing like that. That's day two hundred eighteen.

sources.q: Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not; for of such is the kingdom of God.
And embracing them, and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them.
